newsitem.title: CONGO: Sixth day of Brazzaville clashes, foreigners flee.
newsitem.headline: Sixth day of Brazzaville clashes, foreigners flee.

text.p: Gunfire rattled through Brazzaville for a sixth day on Tuesday as French soldiers moved through the city rescuing foreigners trapped by fighting.

Bloody street battles between soldiers and militiamen loyal to President Pascal Lissouba and a political militia loyal to ex-president Denis Sassou Nguesso have ebbed and flowed through the city centre since Thursday.
Hundreds of Congolese civilians took refuge in the Bacongo suburb, fief of a neutral militia loyal to Mayor Bernard Kolelas, who has offered to mediate between the two sides.
Light armoured cars protected convoys of civilian vehicles driven by French, Lebanese and other expatriate volunteers as they moved to different parts of the city centre.

France has sent 400 troops to reinforce the 450 already in Brazzaville, where they were sent in March in case foreigners needed to be evacuated from Kinshasa, the neighbouring capital of Laurent Kabila's Congo.

French embassy officials said between 700 and 800 foreigners were flown out of Brazzaville on Monday in Transall military transport planes to the Gabon capital Libreville. They said more than 1,000 French citizens could still be in the Brazzaville area.
"I'm just so relieved to be here in the embassy," said one Canadian woman who was beaten up by Congolese troops who spotted her trying to film them from her flat.
Some seemed more concerned about their pets than themselves. Every time they heard a shell landing outside, one Russian couple threw themselves on their dachsund dogs to protect them.
"For us personally this has been a thousand times worse than when we were brought out of Rwanda in 1994," said Leen Jakobs, a Belgian woman.
A column of smoke rose near to the tower housing the offices of French oil company Elf Aquitaine, and the sound of heavy firing could be heard coming from there.
Political and ethnic conflict which killed 2,000 people in the capital in 1993 has exploded again as Congo approached a presidential election set for July 27.

The government, enforcing a crackdown on private militias after clashes in the north, sent troops on Thursday to surround the home of Sassou Nguesso, who lost the last presidential election to Lissouba in 1992.
It was not clear which fighters controlled what territory, despite a claim broadcast on the state radio frequency on Monday night that Sassou Nguesso's men controlled most of the city.

"There was a push by Sassou's forces yesterday (Monday) and they got close to the town hall but the government forces counter-attacked and seem to have pushed them back," said Captain Alexis Jaraud, spokesman for French forces in Congo.

On Monday, French President Jacques Chirac's spokeswoman said Chirac had received verbal agreement for a truce in telephone conversations with Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso, and they would accept mediation from Gabonese President Omar Bongo.
The message appeared not to have reached the fighters on the ground.

"The heavy weaponry that is being used, particularly multiple rocket launchers, must be causing very heavy civilian casualties but the death toll is unknown because foreign military and aid workers cannot reach many of the areas under fire," said a Western military source in Brazzaville.

Jaraud said the oil town of Pointe Noire was unaffected by the fighting and some people were being evacuated there. An executive of Elf Aquitaine in Paris said oil production and exports were unaffected by the fighting in the capital.

Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of the Congo said a shell which landed across the river in Kinshasa from fighting in Brazzaville on Monday was a deliberate act of provocation. It fell in the garden of a Nigerian diplomat causing little damage.
